reference.source: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Classified as external, internal or intra-articular, and defining the type clinically directs both investigation and treatment.
External coxa saltans is a palpable or visible lateral snap as the posterior iliotibial band or anterior border of gluteus maximus flips over the greater trochanter during flexion and extension.

Internal coxa saltans is an audible or palpable groin clunk from the iliopsoas tendon catching over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head as the hip moves from flexion-abduction-external rotation into extension.
Intra-articular snapping from a labral tear, loose body or chondral flap produces true mechanical clicking and warrants intra-articular imaging.
The snapping itself is frequently painless; it becomes symptomatic once secondary bursitis or tendinopathy develops.
It is common in dancers, gymnasts, runners and young women, and is often bilateral.
Dynamic ultrasound is the investigation of choice for internal and external types because it demonstrates the abnormal tendon movement in real time.
Management is predominantly conservative with stretching and physiotherapy; iliopsoas or iliotibial band lengthening is reserved for painful cases refractory to non-operative treatment.
reference.pathophysiology: Coxa saltans occurs when a musculotendinous structure abruptly catches and releases over a bony prominence. In the external type the posterior iliotibial band or the anterior edge of gluteus maximus snaps across the greater trochanter during hip flexion and extension, often provoking overlying trochanteric bursitis. In the internal type the iliopsoas tendon snaps over the iliopectineal eminence, femoral head or lesser trochanter as the hip transitions from a flexed, abducted, externally rotated position into extension and internal rotation. Intra-articular snapping reflects mechanical derangement within the joint such as a labral tear, loose body or synovial chondromatosis. Repetitive snapping incites peritendinous inflammation, bursal thickening and tendinopathy that convert a painless mechanical phenomenon into a painful syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome / trochanteric bursitis
Intra-articular loose body or synovial chondromatosis
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic ultrasound of the iliopsoas tendon and the lateral peritrochanteric structures
MRI or MR arthrography to identify intra-articular causes and associated bursitis
Radiographs to exclude bony abnormality, loose bodies and proximal femoral morphology
Image-guided diagnostic injection of the iliopsoas sheath or trochanteric bursa
Dynamic iliopsoas assessment or bursography where ultrasound is inconclusive
redFlags: Snapping accompanied by locking or giving way, suggesting intra-articular derangement or a loose body
Progressive, rest or night pain rather than mechanical, activity-related symptoms
New snapping after hip surgery or trauma, suggesting tendon subluxation or hardware impingement
Fixed deformity or restricted rotation indicating an alternative structural diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, as most cases are painless or settle with stretching and activity modification. Surgical lengthening for refractory painful snapping is usually successful but carries a risk of transient hip flexor or abductor weakness and occasional recurrence.
pitfalls: Assuming that all snapping is pathological, when a painless snap in a young athlete frequently requires only reassurance.
Missing an intra-articular cause by omitting arthrography or arthroscopic assessment in true mechanical clicking.
Over-releasing the iliopsoas and producing symptomatic hip flexor weakness.
Proceeding to surgery without first clearly distinguishing internal from external snapping by dynamic examination and ultrasound.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: First-line conservative management with activity modification, relative rest and physiotherapy targeting iliotibial band and iliopsoas stretching with hip strengthening
Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain from secondary bursitis or tendinopathy
Image-guided corticosteroid injection into the trochanteric bursa or iliopsoas sheath for refractory inflammatory pain, which also confirms the source
Direct treatment to the snapping type, distinguishing external iliotibial or gluteus maximus snapping over the greater trochanter from internal iliopsoas snapping over the iliopectineal eminence
Surgical iliotibial band lengthening or iliopsoas tendon lengthening for painful snapping refractory to conservative measures
Hip arthroscopy to address intra-articular causes such as a labral tear, loose body or chondral flap
Counsel the patient on the risk of transient hip flexor or abductor weakness and occasional recurrence after surgery
